paper: Ding & Do 2025, APL Machine Learning 3, 036112 — Deciphering the small-angle scattering of polydisperse hard spheres using deep learning (OSTI 3002302)
domain: Small-angle scattering (SANS/SAXS) inversion for polydisperse hard-sphere colloidal suspensions
verdict_context: REPLICATED (core NN inferrer+generator claims confirmed on all 3 distribution families; NN beats PY/PYβ analytic baseline by 17–120× in log₁₀-space MSE).

open_questions.q: Do the trained networks retain their sub-1% inversion accuracy when applied to real experimental SANS/SAXS data on well-characterized polydisperse hard-sphere-like colloids (e.g., silica or PS-latex with independent DLS/TEM sizing), rather than only on the synthetic LAMMPS-derived in-distribution test set?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md §5 verdict and Critique #2 note that all reported accuracy (η R²≈0.9999, σ R²≈0.9998, sub-1% rel-err) is measured on synthetic I(Q) drawn from the same distribution used to train. The paper (per REPORT.md §1) never validates on experimental data, so real-world inversion performance is unknown. This is a genuinely open question: the answer could be anywhere from 'still excellent' (if the physics generalizes) to 'noticeably degraded' (if experimental noise, background, or non-hard-sphere interactions dominate).
next_steps: Locate a public benchmark SANS/SAXS dataset with an independent size distribution measurement (e.g., a NIST SRM colloidal standard, or a Kotlarchyk–Chen-style silica series).
Run the released Inferrer on the experimental I(Q) after resampling to the paper's 100-point Q∈[3,13] reduced grid.
Compare inferred (η,σ) against the independently measured values; report bias and relative error.

open_questions.q: How does the NN generator's 17–120× advantage over PY/PYβ shrink when compared against stronger analytic polydisperse baselines (Vrij 1979 polydisperse PY, Kotlarchyk–Chen 1983 local monodisperse approximation, or Griffith 1987) rather than against the monodisperse-decoupling PY reference used in the paper?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md Claims table C3 and Results §4.2 report NN vs PY and PY+β only. The critique flagged that the SAS community has published stronger polydisperse-aware analytic frameworks that specifically address the high-η, high-σ regime where the paper's PY baseline is known to fail. Whether the NN still wins by 1–2 orders of magnitude, or only by a small factor, against a fair analytic baseline is an unanswered scientific question that materially affects the practical value of the deep-learning approach.
next_steps: Implement Vrij 1979 polydisperse Percus–Yevick S(Q) and Kotlarchyk–Chen LMA in the same evaluation harness used in this replication.
Re-run the MSE_log10 comparison on the released 1000-point test set for all three pdTypes.
Report the reduced advantage factor (NN vs strongest analytic reference) alongside the paper's original PY/PYβ numbers.

open_questions.q: What is the inferrer's accuracy degradation under realistic experimental noise (Poisson counting statistics on I(Q)) and instrumental resolution smearing (e.g., a Gaussian ΔQ/Q of a few percent typical of SANS instruments), and is there a Poisson noise level or resolution width at which the sub-1% rel-err collapses toward the analytic baselines?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md Critique #4 identifies that training I(Q) curves are noiseless simulated intensities on a fixed 100-point reduced-Q grid, while real SANS measurements always carry counting statistics, background subtraction error, and resolution smearing. The 0.34–0.49% relative-error figures cannot be assumed to survive on noisy data. This is cheap to test in silico and is a load-bearing question for any practical deployment.
next_steps: Inject synthetic Poisson noise at counting levels of 10³, 10⁴, 10⁵, 10⁶ counts/point onto the released test-set I(Q).
Convolve with a Gaussian resolution kernel of ΔQ/Q ∈ {1%, 3%, 5%, 10%}.
Re-evaluate inferrer η/σ rel-err vs noise level and resolution; identify the SNR / resolution threshold at which NN accuracy ceases to dominate PYβ.

open_questions.q: Is the 3-dimensional latent space genuinely necessary and sufficient (paper's C4, unverified in this replication), and do the three latent axes admit a physically interpretable decomposition — e.g., one axis for η, one for σ, and one residual — or is the latent entangled?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md Claims table C4 is explicitly listed as 'not tested (architecture accepted from code)' and the LLM-judge verdict flagged it as the main untested claim ('PCA/SVD claim untested'). The paper's Fig 4 argues via SVD/PCA that 3 dimensions suffice; this replication did not re-verify. A follow-up bearing on the interpretability and minimality of the learned representation is a real open question with direct scientific implications for how much information I(Q) carries about (η,σ) in this system.
next_steps: Recompute SVD/PCA on the released 4000-point training I(Q) matrix and report the singular-value spectrum.
Sweep the latent dimensionality (d=1..8), retrain the VAE, and measure inferrer/generator quality as a function of d to test the 'sufficiency' claim empirically.
For d=3, correlate each latent axis with (η,σ,residual) using a linear probe to assess interpretability / entanglement.

open_questions.q: Does the encoder provide calibrated posterior uncertainty on (η,σ) — i.e., can the variance of the latent sampling be propagated into a meaningful predictive credible interval, especially in the physically ill-conditioned regime η→0 (where S(Q)→1 and σ becomes degenerate with a diameter rescaling)?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md Critique #5 notes that the VAE encoder is stochastic (samples ε from N(μ,s²)), so a predictive distribution over (η,σ) is available in principle, but the paper reports only point estimates. Because inversion of polydisperse hard-sphere I(Q) is known to be ill-conditioned in certain (η,σ) regimes, whether the model's implicit uncertainty is well-calibrated (matches true error bars) or overconfident is an unresolved and scientifically important question.
next_steps: Use the released encoder to draw M=100 latent samples per test I(Q); pass each through the L2P converter to get a predictive distribution over (η,σ).
Compute empirical coverage of the resulting credible intervals (e.g., do 68% intervals cover ~68% of true values?) as a calibration diagnostic.
Stratify calibration by (η,σ) region — with particular attention to the low-η and low-σ boundaries — to identify where the model is over- or under-confident.
